item.description:
作者：Guillermo Rauch 账号：@rauchg 简介：@vercel CEO
Most token aggregators have extreme noise from ① token promos from/to providers that train on your data or ② providers that *claim* to be ZDR.
Vercel AI Gateway is the largest trustworthy datasource to understand global AI token flows, because we have real usage, from real customers, an at-scale platform (400k+ paying customers and thousands of enterprises), and zero markup.
Notably… every week we turn down "free token" promos from companies that come to us with dubious claims of Zero Data Retention (ZDR) and questionable reputations. We also don't get a kick out of having the "most providers". Most providers suck. You want the *best* providers.
We put in as much work in engineering our gateway, as in our legal, compliance, privacy, and backoffice operations to responsibly serve trillions of tokens every day. We're here for the long haul.

item.title: I asked Secretary Duffy what Americans should be able to do, if we get this decade right, that they can't do today. Sean Duffy is the Secretary of Transportation, and he sat down with me at our Startup Industrial Base event in DC today. He went straight to how our country's air traffic gets managed...
item.description:
作者：Garry Tan 账号：@garrytan 简介：President & CEO @ycombinator —Founder @garryslist—Creator of GStack & GBrain—designer/engineer who helps founders—SF Dem accelerating the boom loop
I asked Secretary Duffy what Americans should be able to do, if we get this decade right, that they can't do today.
Sean Duffy is the Secretary of Transportation, and he sat down with me at our Startup Industrial Base event in DC today. He went straight to how our country's air traffic gets managed.
At the command center, people sit in front of six screens with a paper flight chart above them, trying to make the calls on weather and routing.
His example: four planes reach the same runway at the same time and only one can land. See it two hours out, speed up two, slow one down, and each one lands when the runway is open. "Like, not complicated stuff, but we don't do any of this."
Paper and pencil and minimal human augmentation from software looks like this: Say an airport can take 15 planes in a 15 minute window. "Well, the airlines will schedule 32." He says he's handing the airlines that data and asking them to spread out.
The tool is SMART, from Air Space Intelligence, a small company he says competed with the biggest companies and won. It predicts. His stage example: a 2.5 hour ground stop might only need 45 minutes. He's taken heat for supposedly handing air traffic control to AI. Duffy's answer? "it's dumb AI, not smart AI." Controllers still make every call.
None of this needs a breakthrough. It needs the will of the people to know they need to use software and be ok with AI augmentation instead of insisting on a paper chart and copper wire.

item.title: How Sam Altman Uses Dots to Take Back His Time
item.description:
播客：AI & I by Every
Do you do all your prompting on Ultrafast?
I do.
That's sick.
Yeah.
That's crazy.
You know, seven people's dots can, working together, create something new that kind of existed in all of our heads to some degree, but was like an emergent thing.
Hey, this is Dan Shipper.
You might be wondering what happened to AI and I.
This is the same show, we are just rebranding it to the Every Podcast.
I'm really excited for our first episode with Sam Waltman.
Here it is.
Sam, welcome to the show.
Thanks for having me.
Psyched to have you here.
So we're here at Dev Day.
I think if you had told me four years ago that the coding models were at this level of capability, I would have been like, wow, I don't know if there would be a lot of developers at Dev Day.
but there's more developers than ever, it seems like, and more work to do than ever.
So what has the, like, riding the increasing capabilities of coding models and seeing the impact on engineering taught you about the future of engineering and more broadly, like, the future of work with AI?
I think people just want so much more stuff.
People's expectations are so high.
And I think that's a wonderful thing.
I think this is why we'll all have this incredible future in front of us to explore.
But developers, they've never been able to do more, but there's never been a higher bar either.
And I think that's great.
I think that's like a nice thing about society.
Is that something that surprised you?
Did you expect that to happen?
I think I was never as doomery about the job stuff as other people, but it still has surprised me somewhat on the upside of just how much latent demand existed in the world and also how much people have remained at the center of everything that is happening with AI.
Do you think there's a limit to that, or do you think that translates pretty cleanly to other areas of work?
I think there will be some areas of work
where there's actually not much creativity required and we don't care about the person doing it.
And many of those tasks or jobs will be done by AI.
But I think there's so much other stuff people want in the world, there's gonna be no shortage of new things to go do.
I think that's been one of the lessons of recent time.
Why do you think it's so human-centered even though we talk a lot about automation?
I mean, one observation is we just, we don't care that much about what the machines do.
And in some sense we never have.
And we're just like, we're obsessed with other people.
We want to know about the person behind the art or the person behind the company or the idea or the product.
And I think this is like a wonderful, positive surprise that we probably should have all known before.
I agree.
I've been thinking, if an agent solves a Navier Stokes in a data center, but no one finds out, did it really solve it?
You know?
I think that was a great example where 10,000 agents worked super hard for four days in perfect coordination with each other and did this amazing thing.
And almost none of the public reaction was about that actually the problem being solved.
A lot of talk about the interpretation, a lot of talk about like the people involved in it in different ways.
That was a good thing.
Yeah.
So it's Dev Day.
You launched, by my count, 22 new things today.
Which I've been at all four Dev Days.
And I think last year was like nine.
And the year before that was like four or five.
So it's a lot more than usual.
Just wait for next year.
OK.
I'm tired.
I'm tired.
We cut a bunch of things that we were going to launch today just because you have to fit it in the 50 minutes.
But we were going to launch a lot of things.
try to practice what we preach.
And if we are saying these tools can make people much more productive and build more and that people want more stuff, like, we better build more ourselves.
What are the new kind of bottlenecks and best practices for doing that?
Because I can see for myself, and I assume you guys are seeing this too, like, now that you can build everything, you're like, what should we build and how do we make it all coherent?
How do you think about that?
Moving to...
this world of sort of persistent intelligence, active intelligence, whatever people wanna call it, this idea that you're gonna have these agents that are running in the background 24 seven, connected to your systems, doing stuff proactively for you.
This is clearly a direction that feels important to explore.
I think we're gonna see amazing stuff happen there.
Another thing we really wanted to do is there's just, there are now so many ideas that are capable of being built and what we are missing is the creative spirit
to figure them out and build them.
So we wanted to really open up our ecosystem, let people build apps in ChatGPT in the same way that we get to do them, let people bring their subscription wherever they'd like, have the marketplace, and really try to let people get connected to all the stuff that people will now be able to build.
Yeah, I mean, just looking at all the platform features that you launched and the way that you talk about platforms, it reminds me a lot of the way that Bill Gates used to talk about Windows as a platform, where you create more value than you capture.
What have you learned, you know, you said this in your keynote and I've observed it as well, there's, at DevDay, there's always an app store.
You've been taking swings at app stores for a while.
What have you learned about building a platform and what do you think makes this one different?
I mean, we clearly have not yet figured out the App Store equivalent, but we have figured out how to build a platform that a lot of people are building incredible value on top of.
I think there are really kind of two schools of thought among people building AI model companies.
There are people that believe or hope that there's only going to be one company in the world.
And then there are people like us that believe we are going to see a renaissance in the number of companies and just an absolute...
lowering of the bar to people, one-person companies, small team companies, creating incredible new products and services.
And we want to go as hard as we can with the platform to enable people to do that.
And although I think we haven't figured out the App Store yet, that's totally fair.
I think we have figured out how to help millions of people build and create significant new products and companies.
If you had to narrow in, you said you talked at the keynote about an industrial revolution versus a renaissance, which you just mentioned now.
If you had to narrow in on the key things that make the difference between those two worlds and maybe opening the eyes part in it, but maybe even the broader ecosystem, what do you think those things are?
One take on this would be that the renaissance was fundamentally centered around people and the industrial revolution was fundamentally centered around machines.
There were a lot of good things about the Industrial Revolution.
It had a hugely positive impact on the world in many ways.
But I think a lot of people did not have a purely positive personal impact from that.
And this feeling that people had these like rich lives and did all these things.
And yeah, of course, they like struggled and wanted more and better stuff.
And that's the part the Industrial Revolution did deliver in some ways.
But they were kind of turned into, in many cases,
It's like cog in a machine doing some extremely specialized thing and kind of like disconnected from a lot of the parts that made life good.
I get sad to hear people talk about like, oh, AI is going to automate everything.
There's going to be no role for humans.
We're going to be like,
house cats and the AI will decide how to reward us and tell us what to do.
I have heard people say that.
That's certainly not what we think.
Yeah.

item.description:
作者：Aaron Levie 账号：@levie 简介：ceo @box - your business lives in content. unleash it with AI
There's a huge opportunity right now in being the deployment layer for AI into the economy. The amount of work it takes to change out workflows in enterprises tends to be far greater than anyone realizes or would prefer. Clearly this is what the applied layer of AI is going to look like in the form of software and agents, but also it opens up new services firms opportunities.
Legacy systems need to be moved to the cloud, data organization and access needs to be updated, software needs to be connected to agents in new ways, workflows need to be reengineered for agents, HITL needs to be figured out for the process, evals need to be generated and maintained, and the entire system needs to be continually updated as new models get released and new capabilities emerge. And the full list may even be longer.
AI is not the same as just deploying software. Software you generally did the implementation of an existing, well understood category of technology, then stepped back and the customer kept running. With AI agents, you're delivering actual work augmentation to the organization, which has a completely different set of complexities associated with it. You're no longer deploying tools that the company is merely enabled by, you're deploying work output in a process. Completely different implementation and enablement process.
As a result, this is going to open up lots of new kinds of firms and plays for existing firms to diffuse AI into organizations. We're going to see approaches by industry, by size of company, and by problem inside of companies. Traditional SIs will modernize and adapt (some will clearly not adapt as well), and new entrants will also be founded in this period that take advantage of this window. Great time to be an FDE or FDE firm.

It’s interesting to contrast, what different companies take for granted in their internal cultures
I’ve only been at OpenAI for about a week, and the thing that stands out is absurdly high bias towards action
This shows up in ways big and small…
Sometimes you have a casual discussion about a possible feature, and the PR is sitting in front of you by the time you get back to your desk
Or you meet someone on Slack and say: “let’s grab lunch next week” and the meeting invites on your calendar within the next five minutes
This has its downsides. because it often feels like everything’s behind a hair trigger, and things just change out from under you— but you can’t really teach this energy, and if you ever lose it, it’s unbelievably hard to get it back
Open AI is not a tiny company anymore. It’s got several massive buildings in San Francisco, it’s impressive that this energy still persists
